name: Felicia And The Pot Of Pinks

pages.caption: Once upon a time there was a poor laborer who, feeling that he had not much longer to live, wished to divide his possessions between his son and daughter, whom he loved dearly.
pages.description: [A poor cottage in a humble village]
pages.scene: A poor cottage in a humble village

pages.caption: So he called them to him, and said: "Your mother brought me as her dowry two stools and a straw bed; I have, besides, a hen, a pot of pinks, and a silver ring, which were given me by a noble lady who once lodged in my poor cottage."
pages.scene: The laborer on his deathbed

pages.caption: When she went away she said to me: "Be careful of my gifts, good man; see that you do not lose the ring or forget to water the pinks. As for your daughter, I promise you that she shall be more beautiful than anyone you ever saw in your life; call her Felicia, and when she grows up give her the ring and the pot of pinks to console her for her poverty."
pages.scene: The noble lady departing the cottage

pages.caption: "Take them both, then, my dear child," he added, "and your brother shall have everything else." The two children seemed quite contented, and when their father died they wept for him, and divided his possessions as he had told them.
pages.scene: Felicia receives the ring and pinks

pages.caption: Felicia believed that her brother loved her, but when she sat down upon one of the stools he said angrily: "Keep your pot of pinks and your ring, but let my things alone. I like order in my house."
pages.scene: Bruno scowling at Felicia

pages.caption: Felicia, who was very gentle, said nothing, but stood up crying quietly; while Bruno, for that was her brother's name, sat comfortably by the fire.
pages.scene: Felicia standing and crying quietly

pages.caption: Presently, when supper-time came, Bruno had a delicious egg, and he threw the shell to Felicia, saying: "There, that is all I can give you; if you don't like it, go out and catch frogs; there are plenty of them in the marsh close by."
pages.description: [Bruno eating an egg, tossing shell to Felicia]
pages.scene: Bruno eating an egg, tossing shell to Felicia

pages.caption: Felicia did not answer, but she cried more bitterly than ever, and went away to her own little room. She found it filled with the sweet scent of the pinks, and, going up to them, she said sadly: "Beautiful pinks, you are so sweet and so pretty, you are the only comfort I have left."
pages.description: [Felicia alone in her small room with pinks]
pages.scene: Felicia alone in her small room with pinks

pages.caption: As she leaned over them she noticed that they were very dry. So taking her pitcher, she ran off in the clear moonlight to the fountain, which was at some distance.
pages.scene: Felicia tending to her dry pinks

pages.caption: When she reached it she sat down upon the brink to rest, but she had hardly done so when she saw a stately lady coming toward her, surrounded by numbers of attendants.
pages.scene: Felicia at the fountain in moonlight

pages.caption: Six maids of honor carried her train, and she leaned upon the arm of another. When they came near the fountain a canopy was spread for her, under which was placed a sofa of cloth-of-gold.
pages.scene: The Queen arriving with her retinue

pages.caption: Presently a dainty supper was served, upon a table covered with dishes of gold and crystal, while the wind in the trees and the falling water of the fountain murmured the softest music.
pages.scene: The Queen at her golden table

pages.caption: Felicia was hidden in the shade, too much astonished by all she saw to venture to move; but in a few moments the Queen said: "I fancy I see a shepherdess near that tree; bid her come hither."
pages.scene: Felicia steps from the shadows

pages.caption: So Felicia came forward and saluted the Queen timidly, but with so much grace that all were surprised. "What are you doing here, my pretty child?" asked the Queen. "Are you not afraid of robbers?"
pages.scene: Felicia salutes the Queen

pages.caption: "Ah! madam," said Felicia, "a poor shepherdess who has nothing to lose does not fear robbers." "You are not very rich, then?" said the Queen, smiling. "I am so poor," answered Felicia, "that a pot of pinks and a silver ring are my only possessions in the world."
pages.scene: Felicia and the Queen talk

pages.caption: "But you have a heart," said the Queen. "What should you say if anybody wanted to steal that?" "I do not know what it is like to lose one's heart, madam," she replied; "but I have always heard that without a heart one cannot live."
pages.description: [The Queen questions Felicia about her heart]
pages.scene: The Queen questions Felicia about her heart

pages.caption: The Queen ordered that a place should be made for her at the table, and herself loaded Felicia's plate with good things; but she was too much astonished to be hungry.
pages.scene: Felicia dines at the Queen's table

pages.caption: "I want to know what you were doing at the fountain so late?" said the Queen presently. "I came to fetch a pitcher of water for my pinks, madam." But when she showed it to the Queen she was amazed to see that it had turned to gold, all sparkling with great diamonds.
pages.scene: Felicia's pitcher transformed to gold

pages.caption: "It is yours, Felicia; go and water your pinks with it, and let it remind you that the Queen of the Woods is your friend." The shepherdess threw herself at the Queen's feet, and thanked her humbly for her gracious words.
pages.scene: The Queen presents the magical pitcher

pages.caption: "Ah! madam," she cried, "if I might beg you to stay here a moment I would run and fetch my pot of pinks for you." "Go, Felicia," said the Queen, stroking her cheek softly; "I will wait here until you come back."
pages.scene: Felicia hurries back to her room

pages.caption: So Felicia took up her pitcher and ran to her little room, but while she had been away Bruno had gone in and taken the pot of pinks, leaving a great cabbage in its place. When she saw the unlucky cabbage Felicia was much distressed.
pages.description: [Felicia discovers the pot is gone, a cabbage in its place]
pages.scene: Felicia discovers the pot is gone, a cabbage in its place

pages.caption: But at last she ran back to the fountain, and, kneeling before the Queen, said: "Madam, Bruno has stolen my pot of pinks, so I have nothing but my silver ring; but I beg you to accept it as a proof of my gratitude."
pages.scene: Felicia kneels before the Queen

pages.caption: So the Queen took the ring and put it on her finger, and mounted her chariot, which was made of coral studded with emeralds, and drawn by six milk-white horses. And Felicia looked after her until the winding of the forest path hid her from her sight.
pages.description: [The Queen departs in her coral chariot]
pages.scene: The Queen departs in her coral chariot

pages.caption: The first thing she did when she reached her room was to throw the cabbage out of the window. But she was very much surprised to hear an odd little voice cry out: "Oh! I am half killed!" and could not tell where it came from.
pages.description: [Felicia throws the cabbage out the window]
pages.scene: Felicia throws the cabbage out the window

pages.caption: As soon as it was light, Felicia, who was very unhappy about her pot of pinks, went out to look for it, and the first thing she found was the unfortunate cabbage. She gave it a push with her foot, saying: "What are you doing here?"
pages.description: [Felicia finds the cabbage in the garden]
pages.scene: Felicia finds the cabbage in the garden

pages.caption: "If I hadn't been carried," replied the cabbage, "you may be very sure that I shouldn't have thought of going there. If you will be good enough to plant me by my comrades again, I can tell you where your pinks are at this moment--hidden in Bruno's bed!"
pages.scene: The cabbage speaks to Felicia

pages.caption: But she replanted the cabbage very kindly in his old place, and, as she finished doing it, she saw Bruno's hen, and said, catching hold of it: "Come here, horrid little creature! you shall suffer for all the unkind things my brother has done to me."
pages.scene: Felicia catches Bruno's hen

pages.caption: "Ah! shepherdess," said the hen, "don't kill me; I am rather a gossip, and I can tell you some surprising things. Don't imagine that you are the daughter of the poor laborer; your mother was a queen who had six girls already."
pages.description: [The hen tells Felicia her true story]
pages.scene: The hen tells Felicia her true story

pages.caption: So when the Queen had another little daughter she was quite frightened, and agreed with her sister (who was a fairy) to exchange her for the fairy's little son. Now the Queen had been shut up in a great tower by the King's orders.
pages.scene: The Queen imprisoned in a tower

pages.caption: When a great many days went by and still she heard nothing from the Fairy she made her escape from the window by means of a rope ladder, taking her little baby with her. After wandering about until she was half dead with cold and fatigue she reached this cottage.
pages.scene: The Queen escapes with her baby

pages.caption: I was the laborer's wife, and was a good nurse, and the Queen gave you into my charge, and told me all her misfortunes, and then died before she had time to say what was to become of you.
pages.description: [The Queen gives baby Felicia to the nurse]
pages.scene: The Queen gives baby Felicia to the nurse

pages.caption: As I never in all my life could keep a secret, I could not help telling this strange tale to my neighbors. One day a beautiful lady came here, and I told it to her also. She touched me with a wand, and instantly I became a hen.
pages.description: [The fairy transforms the nurse into a hen]
pages.scene: The fairy transforms the nurse into a hen

pages.caption: While she was in the house twenty-five of the King's guards came to search for you, doubtless meaning to kill you; but she muttered a few words, and immediately they all turned into cabbages. It was one of them whom you threw out of your window yesterday.
pages.description: [The fairy turns the soldiers into cabbages]
pages.scene: The fairy turns the soldiers into cabbages

pages.caption: Bruno had gone out into the forest, never thinking that Felicia would search in his room for the pinks, and she was delighted by his unexpected absence, and thought to get them back without further trouble.
pages.description: [Felicia searches Bruno's room for the pinks]
pages.scene: Felicia searches Bruno's room for the pinks

pages.caption: But as soon as she entered the room she saw a terrible army of rats, who were guarding the straw bed; and when she attempted to approach it they sprang at her, biting and scratching furiously.
pages.description: [A terrible army of rats guards the pinks]
pages.scene: A terrible army of rats guards the pinks

pages.caption: Then she suddenly bethought herself of the pitcher of water, and, hoping that it might have some magic power, she ran to fetch it, and sprinkled a few drops over the fierce-looking swarm of rats. In a moment not a tail or a whisker was to be seen.
pages.description: [Felicia sprinkles water from the golden pitcher]
pages.scene: Felicia sprinkles water from the golden pitcher

pages.caption: So the Princess could safely take her pot of pinks. She found them nearly dying for want of water, and hastily poured all that was left in the pitcher upon them.
pages.scene: Felicia recovers her pot of pinks

pages.caption: As she bent over them, enjoying their delicious scent, a soft voice, that seemed to rustle among the leaves, said: "Lovely Felicia, the day has come at last when I may have the happiness of telling you how even the flowers love you."
pages.scene: The pink speaks to Felicia

pages.caption: The Princess, quite overcome by the strangeness of hearing a cabbage, a hen, and a pink speak, and by the terrible sight of an army of rats, suddenly became very pale, and fainted away.
pages.scene: Felicia faints from shock

pages.caption: At this moment in came Bruno. Working hard in the heat had not improved his temper, and when he saw that Felicia had succeeded in finding her pinks he was so angry that he dragged her out into the garden and shut the door upon her.
pages.scene: Bruno drags Felicia into the garden

pages.caption: The fresh air soon made her open her pretty eyes, and there before her stood the Queen of the Woods, looking as charming as ever. "You have a bad brother," she said; "I saw he turned you out. Shall I punish him for it?"
pages.description: [The Queen of the Woods appears in the garden]
pages.scene: The Queen of the Woods appears in the garden

pages.caption: "Ah! no, madam," she said; "I am not angry with him." "But supposing he was not your brother, after all, what would you say then?" asked the Queen. "Oh! but I think he must be," said Felicia.
pages.scene: Felicia pleads for Bruno

pages.caption: "What!" said the Queen, "have you not heard that you are a Princess?" "I was told so a little while ago, madam, but how could I believe it without a single proof?"
pages.scene: The Queen reveals Felicia's royal birth

pages.caption: She was interrupted at this moment by the arrival of a very handsome young man. He wore a coat of green velvet fastened with emerald clasps, and had a crown of pinks on his head. He knelt upon one knee and kissed the Queen's hand.
pages.scene: The Prince arrives in green velvet

pages.caption: "Ah!" she cried, "my pink, my dear son, what a happiness to see you restored to your natural shape by Felicia's aid!" And she embraced him joyfully. Then, turning to Felicia, she said: "Charming Princess, I know all the hen told you."
pages.scene: The Queen embraces her restored son

pages.caption: You cannot have heard that the zephyrs, to whom was entrusted the task of carrying my son to the tower where the Queen, your mother, so anxiously waited for him, left him instead in a garden of flowers. Whereupon a fairy with whom I had quarrelled changed him into a pink, and I could do nothing to prevent it.
pages.scene: The Queen explains the enchantment

pages.caption: And you see everything has come right, as I hoped it would. Your giving me the silver ring was the sign that the power of the charm was nearly over. So now, my dear Felicia, if you will be married to my son with this silver ring your future happiness is certain.
pages.description: [The Queen offers Felicia's hand to the Prince]
pages.scene: The Queen offers Felicia's hand to the Prince

pages.caption: "It is yours already, lovely Princess!" he cried, taking her hand in his; "but for the horrible enchantment which kept me silent I should have told you long ago how dearly I love you." This made the Princess very happy.
pages.scene: The Prince declares his love

pages.caption: The Queen, who could not bear to see her dressed like a poor shepherdess, touched her with her wand, saying: "I wish you to be attired as befits your rank and beauty." And immediately the Princess's cotton dress became a magnificent robe of silver brocade embroidered with carbuncles.
pages.scene: Felicia transformed into a magnificent robe

pages.caption: With her soft dark hair encircled by a crown of diamonds, from which floated a clear white veil, and her bright eyes, and the charming color in her cheeks, she was altogether such a dazzling sight that the Prince could hardly bear it.
pages.scene: Felicia as a dazzling princess

pages.caption: Just then Bruno, who was going back to his work, came out of the cottage, and thought he must be dreaming when he saw Felicia; but she called him very kindly, and begged the Queen to take pity on him. "What!" she said, "when he was so unkind to you?"
pages.description: [Felicia begs the Queen to forgive Bruno]
pages.scene: Felicia begs the Queen to forgive Bruno

pages.caption: "Ah! madam," said the Princess, "I am so happy that I should like everybody else to be happy too." The Queen kissed her, and said: "Well, to please you, let me see what I can do for this cross Bruno."
pages.scene: Felicia wishes everyone to be happy

pages.caption: And with a wave of her wand she turned the poor little cottage into a splendid palace, full of treasures; only the two stools and the straw bed remained just as they were, to remind him of his former poverty.
pages.scene: The cottage transformed into a palace

pages.caption: Then the Queen touched Bruno himself, and made him gentle and polite and grateful, and he thanked her and the Princess a thousand times. Lastly, the Queen restored the hen and the cabbages to their natural forms, and left them all very contented.
pages.description: [The Queen restores everyone to their true forms]
pages.scene: The Queen restores everyone to their true forms

pages.caption: The Prince and Princess were married as soon as possible with great splendor, and lived happily ever after.
pages.description: [The wedding of the Prince and Princess]
pages.scene: The wedding of the Prince and Princess
